title: Practice Test 6
description: A full-length adaptive digital SAT practice test written by SAT Ustoz: 98 questions, two modules per section, with an explanation for every question.

questions.passage: The warehouse robot's gripper is remarkably ______: in a single shift, it can lift a heavy crate, pick up a grape without bruising it, and fold a cotton shirt.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The gripper handles very different jobs, from heavy crates to delicate grapes, so it is **versatile**.

questions.passage: Author Emily Carter's picture book *The Lantern Moth* is notably ______ with words: most pages hold a single short sentence, leaving the illustrations to tell much of the story.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: One short sentence per page means using few words, so she is **sparing** with them. *Generous* is the opposite.

questions.passage: In parts of Valencia, Spain, the paella served at a large wedding is rarely cooked by the host family. The task is instead ______ to a paellero, a specialist cook whose skill with enormous pans of rice, beans, and meat is known throughout the neighborhood.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The family hands an important job to a trusted specialist, so the task is **entrusted** to the paellero.

questions.passage: Glaciologist Arvid Halvorsen cautions that a single cool summer, which may briefly slow a glacier's retreat, should not be treated as ______ evidence that the glacier is recovering: decades of measurements show the ice thinning steadily despite occasional pauses of this kind.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Halvorsen warns that one cool summer does not settle the question, since long-term data show continued thinning. Evidence that settles a question is **conclusive**. Warning against treating it as *spurious* (false) evidence would mean it is genuine evidence of recovery, the opposite of his point.

questions.passage: For decades, engineers who wanted robots to grasp unfamiliar objects tried to copy the human hand, building fingers with dozens of joints, motors, and sensors. Such hands were expensive and often failed when an object had an unusual shape. __One simpler design does away with fingers entirely: a rubber balloon filled with coffee grounds is pressed against an object, molds around it, and then stiffens when air is pumped out, locking the object in place.__
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes an alternative design that avoids the problems mentioned in the previous sentence.
It gives an example of a robotic hand that closely imitates the human hand.
It explains why engineers stopped trying to build robots that grasp objects.
It identifies a weakness shared by all robotic grippers.
questions.explanation: The previous sentence names the problems with copying the hand; the underlined sentence offers a finger-free design that gets around them.

questions.passage: When author Samuel Price submitted the manuscript of *The Boy Who Counted Clouds*, three publishers rejected it, complaining that the story had no villain and almost no plot: a boy spends one summer on a rooftop in Naples, naming the shapes he sees in the sky. The small press that eventually published the book left its quiet structure unchanged. Teachers soon reported that young readers, with no complicated plot to follow, began inventing cloud stories of their own, and the book has since been reprinted eleven times.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that children's books should never include villains
To describe how small presses decide which manuscripts to publish
To explain why the author chose to set his book in Naples
To show how a feature of a book that publishers considered a weakness turned out to be part of its appeal
questions.explanation: Publishers saw the missing plot as a flaw, yet that same quiet structure let readers invent their own stories, and the book succeeded.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
A layer of rock debris more than a few centimeters thick shields glacier ice from the sun's heat. For this reason, many glaciologists expect glaciers covered in debris to lose ice much more slowly than clean glaciers in the same climate, and some forecasts of future water supply in South Asia treat debris-covered glaciers as relatively secure.

**Text 2**
Satellite measurements analyzed by a team led by geographer Laura Bennett show that debris-covered glaciers in the Himalayas have been thinning at about the same rate as nearby clean glaciers. The team traced much of the loss to scattered ice cliffs and meltwater ponds on the debris-covered surfaces. Although these features occupy only a small share of each glacier, they absorb heat and rapidly melt the surrounding ice.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Bennett's team most likely respond to the forecasts described in Text 1?
choices: By rejecting the idea that a thick layer of debris can insulate the ice beneath it
By suggesting that the forecasts overlook surface features that let heat reach the ice despite the debris, so debris-covered glaciers may be less secure than assumed
By agreeing that debris-covered glaciers lose ice more slowly than clean glaciers, except in the Himalayas
By arguing that ice cliffs and meltwater ponds form mainly on glaciers that have no debris
questions.explanation: Text 2 finds similar thinning and explains it with ice cliffs and ponds, which the forecasts ignore. The team never denies that debris insulates the ice it covers; it points to the small areas where heat gets through, so rejecting insulation outright goes too far.

questions.passage: Account books from a nineteenth-century dye workshop in Avignon show that the color of a silk scarf said a great deal about its price. Red dye came from madder root, which grew nearby, and yellow from local plants such as weld. Deep blue, however, required indigo, which arrived by ship from India, and the workshop charged far more for blue cloth than for red or yellow cloth.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Madder root was the most common plant grown near Avignon.
Silk scarves were worn only by the wealthiest residents of Avignon.
The workshop's prices for dyed cloth reflected whether a dye could be obtained locally or had to be imported.
Indigo was used mainly to dye cotton rather than silk.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts cheap local dyes (red and yellow) with costly imported indigo, which explains the difference in price.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Leo has entered a robot he built in a school competition.

The robot was supposed to sort colored blocks into bins, but halfway through its first round it began spinning in place, scattering blocks across the floor. Leo felt his face grow hot as the judges marked their sheets. Then he noticed a cluster of first-graders pressed against the railing, laughing and cheering each time the robot spun. When the round ended, they begged him to make it dance again, and for the first time all morning, Leo laughed too.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Leo's robot fails at its task, the young spectators' delight helps him enjoy the moment.
Leo realizes that he programmed the robot incorrectly and decides to fix it before the next round.
The judges are impressed by the robot's unexpected spinning.
Leo is annoyed that the first-graders are laughing at his robot.
questions.explanation: Leo is embarrassed at first, but the children's cheering turns the failure into something he can laugh at.

questions.passage: Anthropologist Nikos Pappas, who studies households in mountain villages of northern Greece, argues that families there serve guests freshly baked bread mainly as a sign of respect rather than because they simply prefer fresh bread.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Pappas's argument?
choices: Most households in the villages own a clay oven for baking bread.
Bread baked in the villages stays fresh longer than bread bought in city shops.
Families that ate bread several days old at their own meals still baked fresh bread whenever a guest was expected.
Guests in the villages usually arrive in the late afternoon.
questions.explanation: If families happily eat old bread themselves but still bake fresh bread for guests, the fresh bread is about honoring the guest, not about taste.

questions.passage: "Loom Song" is a poem by Rosa Delgado. In the poem, the speaker suggests that weaving connects her to the women who worked at the loom before her.
questions.prompt: Which quotation from "Loom Song" most effectively illustrates this claim?
choices: "Each knot I pull, my grandmother pulled first; / her patient hands still move inside my own."
"The loom is older than the house it stands in, / its frame gone dark with a century of smoke."
"I choose the red for warmth, the blue for distance, / and let the colors argue on the frame."
"By evening, the shuttle's rhythm slows, / and the courtyard fills with the sound of rain."
questions.explanation: Only this quotation ties the speaker's weaving to an earlier weaver, her grandmother, whose hands she feels in her own. The line about the old loom mentions the past but says nothing about the women who used it.

questions.passage: A geographer studying four glaciers in the same valley suggests that glaciers whose lower ends lie at lower elevations, where the air is warmer, have retreated farther in recent decades. For example, ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: East Glacier retreated 390 meters between 2000 and 2020.
the lower end of North Glacier sits at 3,950 meters, higher than the lower end of East Glacier.
West Glacier, which ends at the highest elevation, retreated farther than North Glacier did.
the lower end of South Glacier sits at 3,210 meters, and that glacier retreated 655 meters, while West Glacier, which ends at 4,120 meters, retreated only 85 meters.
questions.explanation: The example must pair elevation with retreat. South Glacier ends lowest and retreated most; West Glacier ends highest and retreated least. The claim that West retreated farther than North is false: West retreated 85 meters and North 140.

questions.passage: Many robot vacuum cleaners avoid falling down stairs by shining infrared light at the floor and measuring how much of it is reflected back: when little light returns, the robot assumes it has reached a drop-off and backs away. Owners have reported that these robots often refuse to cross very dark rugs, which absorb most of the light that strikes them. This behavior suggests that the robots ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: are unable to detect real staircases.
mistake the dark rugs for drop-offs such as the edge of a staircase.
clean dark rugs more thoroughly than light-colored floors.
rely on cameras rather than infrared light to detect obstacles.
questions.explanation: Dark rugs reflect little light, which is exactly the signal the robot reads as a drop-off, so it backs away from them.

questions.passage: At a site in the Rhône Valley that was occupied for many centuries, archaeologists found charred grape seeds in household hearths from every period. Seeds from the oldest layers are short and round, like those of wild grapes, whereas seeds from more recent layers are longer and narrower, a shape typical of cultivated vines. Because pollen records show that wild grapevines grew in the nearby river forests throughout the site's history, the archaeologists concluded that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: residents most likely stopped eating grapes during the later periods of occupation.
wild grapevines most likely disappeared from the river forests before the site's later periods.
the site's earliest residents most likely grew more cultivated vines than its later residents did.
the change in seed shape most likely reflects residents' growing reliance on cultivated vines rather than the loss of wild grapes from the area.
questions.explanation: Wild grapes stayed available, so their disappearance can't explain the change; residents must have shifted toward cultivated grapes. The option about wild vines disappearing is ruled out by the pollen records.

questions.passage: Molas, the textile panels of Panama's Guna people, are made entirely by ______ their bold patterns are cut from layers of colored cloth and stitched together piece by piece.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Both parts are complete sentences, so they need a semicolon. A comma alone creates a comma splice.

questions.passage: The team's ______ a four-legged machine assembled from recycled bicycle parts, climbed a full flight of stairs during the regional competition.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The phrase "a four-legged machine...parts" renames the robot and closes with a comma, so it must open with a comma too.

questions.passage: The children's ______ *The Salt Road Fox* tells the story of a young fox who follows a camel caravan across the desert in search of her lost brother.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The title identifies which novel is meant, so it is essential and takes no punctuation. A comma would also need a closing comma after the title, and there is none.

questions.passage: In Mei's kitchen, the dough for hand-pulled noodles needs only three ______ wheat flour, water, and salt. The real skill lies in the stretching, which can take years to master.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: A colon introduces the list that names the three ingredients. A semicolon would need a complete sentence after it.

questions.passage: The tiny moons orbiting the distant planet ______ too dim to be seen without a powerful telescope.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "moons," so the verb is **are**.

questions.passage: Since its founding in 1998, the small textile museum ______ more than four hundred embroidered panels from families across Sicily.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "Since its founding" describes an action that began in the past and continues now, so the present perfect **has collected** is needed.

questions.passage: The letters exchanged by the silk merchant and his business partner in Lyon ______ how quickly prices for raw silk rose during the 1870s.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "letters," so the verb is **reveal**. The singular nouns "partner" and "Lyon" sit right before the blank but are not the subject.

questions.passage: Sea ice reflects most of the sunlight that strikes it, while dark ocean water absorbs most of it. ______ as Arctic sea ice melts and exposes more open water, the region absorbs more heat, which in turn melts more ice.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The extra heat absorption is a result of the difference described in the first sentence.

questions.passage: Before the 1800s, weaving a complex pattern on a loom required a helper, often called a draw boy, who raised particular threads by hand for each row. The Jacquard loom, introduced in France in the early 1800s, ______ used chains of punched cards to select the threads automatically, so a single weaver could produce intricate designs.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The Jacquard loom did automatically what earlier looms needed a helper to do, so the sentence contrasts the two.

questions.passage: Engineers acknowledge that humanoid robots, which walk on two legs, are far less efficient than wheeled robots on flat floors. ______ they argue that a robot with legs and arms can work in spaces built for people, climbing stairs and opening doors that would stop a wheeled machine.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The first sentence concedes a weakness; the second gives an advantage anyway, so the concession word **Still** fits. *Indeed* would wrongly signal that the second sentence reinforces the first.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Crackers are thin, crisp baked snacks found in many countries.
• They are typically baked on flat trays in very hot ovens.
• Before baking, bakers punch rows of small holes, called docking holes, into the dough.
• The holes let steam escape, so the crackers bake flat and crisp instead of puffing up into bubbles.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain the purpose of docking holes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Crackers are thin, crisp baked snacks found in many countries.
Crackers are typically baked on flat trays in very hot ovens.
Docking holes are small holes that bakers punch into cracker dough.
Bakers punch docking holes into cracker dough so that steam can escape and the crackers bake flat instead of puffing up.
questions.explanation: Only this choice says what the holes do: they let steam escape so the crackers stay flat. The option that only defines docking holes names them but not their purpose.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• *Little Goat's Long Walk* and *The Apricot Thief* are picture books by author Hannah Moss.
• *Little Goat's Long Walk* was published in 2014.
• *The Apricot Thief* was published in 2019.
• *Little Goat's Long Walk* is written in rhyming verse.
• *The Apricot Thief* is written in prose.
• Both books are set in villages in Cornwall.
questions.prompt: The student wants to contrast the writing styles of the two books. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: *Little Goat's Long Walk* was published in 2014, five years before *The Apricot Thief*.
Both of Moss's picture books, *Little Goat's Long Walk* and *The Apricot Thief*, are set in villages in Cornwall.
Although both are picture books by Moss, *Little Goat's Long Walk* is written in rhyming verse, whereas *The Apricot Thief* is written in prose.
*The Apricot Thief*, a picture book by Moss, is written in prose.
questions.explanation: Writing style means verse versus prose, and a contrast needs both books. The publication dates are a difference, but not one of style, and the option about *The Apricot Thief* alone describes only one book.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Fog nets are large mesh panels set up on hillsides in some dry coastal regions.
• As fog drifts through the mesh, tiny water droplets collect on the fibers.
• The droplets merge, run down the mesh, and drip into gutters below.
• The nets need no electricity.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain how fog nets collect water. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Fog nets are large mesh panels set up on hillsides in some dry coastal regions.
As fog drifts through a fog net's mesh, tiny droplets collect on the fibers, merge, and drip into gutters below.
In some dry coastal regions, fog nets are set up on hillsides.
questions.explanation: Only this choice describes the process by which the nets gather water.

questions.passage: The textile museum's new exhibit is designed to be ______: visitors can touch samples of wool and silk, try a small hand loom, and spin thread on a wooden spindle.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Touching, weaving, and spinning let visitors take part, so the exhibit is **interactive**.

questions.passage: After months of drought, the farmers were ______ when steady rain finally began to fall on their dry fields.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Rain ending a long drought would make farmers feel **relieved**.

questions.passage: The robot's designers made its movements deliberately ______ so that the factory workers beside it could always tell where its arm would go next.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Workers can predict the arm's path only if it always moves the same way, so the movements are **consistent**. *Erratic* is the opposite.

questions.passage: The critic praised the picture book for its ______ humor: its jokes delight young listeners while also offering sly asides that the adults reading aloud will appreciate.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The humor works on two levels, one for children and one for adults, so it is **layered**.

questions.passage: Some engineers design robots that start out as flat sheets and fold themselves into three-dimensional shapes when heated, much like a sheet of paper folded into an origami crane. Because they can be shipped flat, such robots could be sent to remote places, including outer space, while taking up very little storage room.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that robots should be built from paper
To explain how origami cranes are folded
To describe a type of robot and explain one advantage of its design
To compare robots used on Earth with robots used in space
questions.explanation: The text describes self-folding robots and then gives a benefit: they can be shipped flat.

questions.passage: Many picture books for toddlers are printed on thick cardboard pages instead of paper. __These "board books" can survive being chewed, dropped, and bent by small hands that are not yet able to turn thin pages gently.__ Publishers therefore often release popular picture books in board-book editions once the books have proved successful.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains why a type of book is well suited to very young children.
It describes a problem that publishers have not yet solved.
It compares board books with books read on screens.
It argues that toddlers prefer thin paper pages to cardboard ones.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains what makes cardboard pages a good fit for toddlers, which is why publishers make board-book editions.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Some designers of robots for elder care argue that the robots should look as humanlike as possible, since older adults may find a familiar face comforting.

**Text 2**
In a study at a care home, researchers found that most residents preferred a robot shaped like a simple, friendly animal over a robot with a realistic human face. Several residents described the realistic robot as unsettling.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the designers in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that robots for elder care should have realistic human faces
By pointing out that a humanlike appearance may make some older adults uneasy rather than comforted
By arguing that older adults do not want robots in care homes at all
By suggesting that animal-shaped robots are more expensive to build
questions.explanation: Residents found the realistic face unsettling, which challenges the claim that a humanlike look is comforting.

questions.passage: In many traditional Turkish homes, a sofra, a cloth spread on the floor or on a low table, is covered with bread, fruit, nuts, and sweets whenever guests arrive. Hosts set out far more food than visitors could possibly eat, because a full sofra is a way of showing generosity and welcome.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Guests are expected to eat everything placed on the sofra.
A sofra is always spread on the floor rather than on a table.
Bread is the most important food served to guests.
Hosts fill the sofra with plentiful food as a way of showing generosity to guests.
questions.explanation: The text describes the abundant food and explains that it signals generosity and welcome.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Chloe is visiting her aunt's farm for the first time.

Chloe had imagined the farm as a quiet place for reading under fruit trees. Instead, the rooster began shouting before dawn, the goats complained loudly from their pen, and her aunt handed her a bucket before she had finished breakfast. By noon her arms ached, but when her aunt praised the neat rows she had weeded, Chloe felt prouder than she had after any test at school.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although the farm is busier and harder than Chloe expected, the work gives her a new sense of pride.
Chloe is disappointed that she has no time to read on the farm and wants to go home.
Chloe's aunt is unhappy with how slowly Chloe works.
Chloe learns how to care for the goats on her aunt's farm.
questions.explanation: The farm is not the quiet place she pictured, but her aunt's praise for her work leaves her feeling proud.

questions.passage: A student hypothesizes that bean seedlings grown under red light grow taller than bean seedlings grown under blue light.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student's hypothesis?
choices: Seedlings grown under blue light produced more leaves than seedlings grown under red light.
Seedlings grown under red light grew taller, on average, than identical seedlings grown under blue light.
Both groups of seedlings were watered at the same time every day.
Red and blue lights are both commonly used in greenhouses.
questions.explanation: Only this finding compares the heights of the two groups, which is what the hypothesis is about.

questions.passage: Carpet historian Arthur Bell claims that a large nineteenth-century carpet in a museum's collection was woven by several weavers working side by side rather than by a single weaver.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bell's claim?
choices: The carpet's wool was dyed with madder and indigo.
The carpet is one of the largest in the museum's collection.
Carpets of a similar size were often given as wedding gifts.

The knots in the carpet's left, middle, and right sections were tied with three noticeably different techniques, and the borders between these sections run straight from the bottom of the carpet to the top.
questions.explanation: Three knotting styles in side-by-side strips running the whole length of the carpet point to three weavers working next to one another.

questions.passage: A teacher recorded the number of students in a school's robotics club each year from 2021 to 2024. Membership was highest in ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
questions.explanation: 41 is the largest number in the table, and it belongs to 2023.

questions.passage: Glaciers form where snow piles up year after year. Over time, the weight of new snow presses the older layers beneath it into dense ice. Because this process requires more snow to fall each winter than melts the following summer, glaciers are unlikely to form in places where ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: most of each winter's snow melts away during the summer.
snow falls mainly at high elevations.
questions.explanation: If most snow melts each summer, it can't pile up year after year, so no glacier forms.

questions.passage: As mountain glaciers shrink, the amount of meltwater they release each summer may at first increase, since warmer temperatures melt more ice. Eventually, however, a shrinking glacier becomes too small to release as much water as it once did. Communities that depend on rivers fed by glacier meltwater may therefore ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: see river flows decline at first and then recover.
see no change in river flows as the glaciers shrink.
see river flows rise for a time before they begin to decline.
receive more water every year for as long as temperatures keep rising.
questions.explanation: Meltwater first increases and later falls as the glacier gets too small, so river flows would rise and then decline.

questions.passage: Although the apricot orchard was planted only six years ______ it already produces enough fruit to supply the village market.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: A comma separates the introductory "Although..." clause from the main sentence.

questions.passage: Mia's grandmother keeps her spices in small glass ______ each one is labeled in her neat, slanting handwriting.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Both parts are complete sentences, so they need a semicolon. A comma alone creates a comma splice.

questions.passage: Lola's favorite picture book, which her grandfather read to her every ______ is now held together with tape.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The clause "which her grandfather...night" opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "is."

questions.passage: The beginner's robot kit includes a battery ______ two small motors, and a set of light sensors.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Items in a simple list of three are separated by commas.

questions.passage: The baskets woven by the village's craftspeople ______ sold at the weekly market.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "baskets," so the verb is **are**.

questions.passage: During the cotton harvest, many of the region's ______ hire extra workers to bring in the crop before the autumn rains.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a plural noun that simply names the farms, so **farms** fits. Nothing belongs to the farms here, so no apostrophe is needed.

questions.passage: Last spring, the research team ______ a network of sensors across the glacier to record the temperature of the ice.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "Last spring" places the action in the past, so the past tense **installed** fits.

questions.passage: Wool traps air between its fibers, which helps keep heat close to the body. ______ wool has been one of the most common materials for winter clothing for thousands of years.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Wool's warmth is the reason it is used for winter clothing, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

questions.passage: Most robots in factories repeat a single motion thousands of times a day. ______ robots used in hospitals must handle a wide variety of tasks, from delivering medicine to guiding visitors through hallways.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Hospital robots do many different tasks, the opposite of factory robots that repeat one motion.

questions.passage: The illustrator begins every page with a light pencil sketch. ______ she adds watercolor, layering pale washes before painting the darker details.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Adding color is the step that follows the sketch, so a sequence word fits.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Pemmican is a food made from dried meat pounded into a powder and mixed with fat.
• It was developed by Indigenous peoples of North America.
• Because it contains very little water, pemmican can be stored for months without refrigeration.

choices: Pemmican is a food made from dried, pounded meat mixed with fat.
Pemmican was developed by Indigenous peoples of North America.
Because pemmican contains very little water and keeps for months without refrigeration, fur traders could carry it on long journeys.
Fur traders traditionally carried pemmican with them.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Silk is produced by silkworms, which spin cocoons from a single continuous fiber.
• A single silk fiber can be hundreds of meters long.
• Cotton comes from the fluffy fibers that surround the seeds of the cotton plant.
• Cotton fibers are usually only a few centimeters long.

choices: Silk is produced by silkworms, while cotton comes from the cotton plant.
A single silk fiber can be hundreds of meters long, while cotton fibers are usually only a few centimeters long.
Cotton fibers surround the seeds of the cotton plant.
Silkworms spin their cocoons from a single continuous fiber.
questions.explanation: Only this choice compares the lengths of the two fibers. The option about silkworms and the cotton plant contrasts the fibers' sources, not their lengths.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• *The Clever Goat of the Alps* is a children's book by Thomas Keller.
• It was first published in German in 2016.
• It has since been translated into French, Italian, and English.
• Keller worked as a primary school teacher before becoming a writer.
questions.prompt: The student wants to emphasize how widely the book has been translated. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: First published in German, *The Clever Goat of the Alps* has since been translated into French, Italian, and English.
*The Clever Goat of the Alps* was first published in 2016.
Thomas Keller worked as a primary school teacher before writing *The Clever Goat of the Alps*.
*The Clever Goat of the Alps* is a children's book by Thomas Keller.
questions.explanation: Only this choice lists the languages the book has been translated into.

questions.passage: Though the explorer's journals are full of vivid detail, historians regard them as ______ guides to the route he actually traveled: several mountain passes he describes crossing lie more than a hundred kilometers from any path he could have taken.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Passes that lie far from any possible route make the journals untrustworthy as guides, so they are **dubious**. *Meticulous* would mean careful and accurate, the opposite of what the evidence shows.

questions.passage: Critics have sometimes dismissed picture books as slight, but illustrator Nina Petrakis's work resists such ______: her wordless book *Night Ferry* rewards repeated readings, each revealing details in its crowded harbor scenes that earlier viewings missed.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Dismissing picture books as slight is a form of **condescension**, and the colon shows her work proving that attitude wrong. *Scrutiny* doesn't fit: her book actually rewards close looking rather than resisting it.

questions.passage: In her memoir, the weaver describes her apprenticeship with ______ candor: she admits that for her first two years she ruined more cloth than she finished and twice came close to quitting.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: She openly admits unflattering failures, so her candor is **unflinching**. *Selective* would mean she left the embarrassing parts out, which she does not.

questions.passage: The retreat of the Vesla Glacier has not been ______: periods of rapid ice loss in the 1990s and 2010s were separated by a decade in which the glacier's front barely moved.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Fast periods separated by a near pause mean the retreat did not proceed at the same rate throughout, so it has not been **uniform**. *Measurable* is wrong because the text describes measured changes.

questions.passage: Histories of textiles often describe how spinning and weaving machines, beginning in the late 1700s, swept away hand production wherever they appeared. __In some West African towns, however, hand-spinning and hand-weaving remained the main ways of making cloth well into the twentieth century, even as factory-made fabric arrived through trade.__ Scholar Kofi Mensah argues that this persistence reflected not a lack of access to machine-made goods but steady local demand for patterns and textures that factories could not easily copy.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a case that complicates a widely held account, setting up the explanation offered in the next sentence.
It offers further evidence for the account presented in the first sentence.
It explains why factory-made fabric could not reach West African towns.
It summarizes the argument that Mensah makes about local demand.
questions.explanation: The underlined sentence is an exception ("however") to the account that machines swept away handwork, and the next sentence explains that exception. Factory cloth did arrive, so the option saying it could not reach the towns contradicts the text.

questions.passage: Researchers who interviewed owners of robot vacuum cleaners expected to hear the machines described as ordinary appliances, like dishwashers. Instead, many owners reported having named their robots, and some admitted to tidying up before a cleaning run so the robot would not "struggle." The researchers propose that a machine that moves around a home on its own invites people to treat it as something like a companion, even when they know it has no feelings.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a hypothesis, describes evidence that confirms it, and raises a question that remains unanswered.
It identifies a flaw in robot vacuum cleaners and proposes a way to fix it.
It compares robot vacuum cleaners with dishwashers and argues that one is more useful.
It describes an expectation, reports findings that differ from it, and offers an interpretation of those findings.
questions.explanation: The researchers expected owners to treat the robots as appliances, found the opposite ("Instead"), and then explained why. The evidence contradicted the expectation, so the option about confirming a hypothesis is wrong.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Many educators argue that picture books for young children should avoid sad endings. Young children, they reason, may not yet have the emotional tools to cope with loss, and an unresolved sadness can make a story frightening rather than meaningful.

**Text 2**
Children's literature scholar Ruth Adler studied how kindergarten classes responded to picture books that end with a loss, such as the death of a pet. When teachers read the books aloud and then invited discussion, children often connected the stories to their own experiences and talked about them calmly. Adler concludes that what matters is less the ending itself than whether an adult helps children talk about it.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Adler most likely respond to the educators' view in Text 1?
choices: She would argue that sad endings need not overwhelm young children if an adult helps them discuss the stories.
She would agree that sad endings should be avoided unless the books are read at home.
She would argue that young children cope with loss better than adults do.
She would claim that young children generally prefer sad endings to happy ones.
questions.explanation: Adler found that children handled sad endings calmly when adults led a discussion, so the ending alone is not the problem. She makes no comparison with adults and says nothing about which endings children prefer.

questions.passage: Scientists can reconstruct past climates from glacier ice because tiny bubbles in the ice trap samples of the atmosphere from the time the snow fell. In many mountain glaciers, however, summer meltwater seeps down through the snow and refreezes, mixing material from different years and blurring the record. For this reason, researchers seeking long, detailed climate records from mountain ranges often look for glaciers at very high elevations, where temperatures rarely rise above freezing even in summer.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Because melting can blur the climate records stored in glacier ice, researchers seeking detailed records from mountains favor very high, cold glaciers.
Ice from mountain glaciers provides more detailed climate records than ice from any other source.
Bubbles in glacier ice preserve samples of the atmosphere from the time the ice melted.
Summer meltwater has destroyed the climate records in nearly all mountain glaciers.
questions.explanation: The text explains a problem (meltwater blurs the record) and the researchers' response (seeking high, cold glaciers). The option about meltwater destroying nearly all records overstates the text, which says only that it blurs records in many glaciers.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Walter, a retired mapmaker, is looking at a map he drew forty years earlier.

The map had been his finest work: every irrigation canal, every orchard wall, every footpath between the villages traced in ink so fine it seemed breathed onto the paper. Walter unfolded it on the kitchen table and found his own street, then the bend in the canal where the old mill had stood. The mill was gone now, the canal paved over, the orchards divided into building lots. Yet the map, he realized, was not wrong. It was simply loyal to a place that no longer existed.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Walter discovers several errors in a map he once considered his finest work.
Walter realizes that his old map, though it no longer matches the area, faithfully records a place that has since disappeared.
Walter regrets that he never drew a map of the area as it looks today.
Walter decides to redraw the map to show the area's new streets and buildings.
questions.explanation: The landscape has changed, but Walter concludes the map "was not wrong": it is "loyal" to the place as it was. The option about errors contradicts that realization.

questions.passage: Robotics researcher Jonas Berg hypothesizes that pedestrians trust a sidewalk delivery robot more when it signals where it is about to go, for example by projecting arrows onto the pavement, than when it moves without giving such signals.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Berg's hypothesis?
choices: Pedestrians who passed a robot projecting arrows rated it as more trustworthy than did pedestrians who passed an otherwise identical robot that gave no signals.
Pedestrians rated robots that projected arrows as more trustworthy than human couriers on bicycles.
Robots that projected arrows used slightly more battery power than robots that did not.
Most pedestrians in the trials said they had never encountered a delivery robot before.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis compares signaling robots with robots that don't signal, and this finding makes exactly that comparison while keeping everything else the same. Comparing robots with human couriers tests a different question.

questions.passage: Anthropologist Marina Costa surveyed households in four villages (identified here by pseudonyms) in 2005 and again in 2025. In every village, a smaller share of households baked their own bread in 2025 than in 2005, but Costa claims that the decline was steepest in villages located close to a commercial bakery. ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Costa's claim?
choices: In 2005, Meadow had the highest share of households baking their own bread, at 92%.
In 2025, fewer than 90% of households baked their own bread in each of the four villages.
In Orchard, 2 kilometers from a commercial bakery, the share of households baking their own bread fell from 88% to 41%, while in Meadow, 28 kilometers away, it fell only from 92% to 89%.
In Spring, 6 kilometers from a commercial bakery, the share fell from 90% to 63%, a steeper drop than in Orchard.
questions.explanation: The claim links distance to the size of the decline, so the support must compare a near village with a far one. Orchard (2 km) dropped 47 points and Meadow (28 km) only 3. The Spring option is false: its 27-point drop is smaller than Orchard's.
